nameStory: The name "ginkgo" comes from a centuries-old transcription error! The tree was originally known as "silver fruit" or "white fruit" in Chinese, but somewhere along the way, scribes made a mistake that stuck. You might also hear it called the maidenhair tree because its fan-shaped leaves remind people of the delicate fronds of maidenhair ferns.
description: The ginkgo is truly a living dinosaur - a tree that has remained virtually unchanged for over 170 million years! These distinctive trees grow as tall shade trees with a unique, almost prehistoric appearance. Their most famous feature is their fan-shaped leaves that turn brilliant golden-yellow in fall. Ginkgos are tough city trees that can live for thousands of years and tolerate pollution better than most species.

idTips.label: Fan-shaped leaves
idTips.description: The leaves look like little green fans or duck feet, completely unlike any other tree. They feel smooth and leathery to the touch, with parallel veins that fork repeatedly from the base - no central midrib like most leaves.

idTips.label: Clustered leaf arrangement
idTips.description: Leaves grow in tight clusters on short spurs along the branches, creating a distinctive bunched appearance rather than being evenly spaced.

idTips.label: Golden fall color
idTips.description: In autumn, the entire tree transforms into a brilliant golden-yellow beacon that's visible from blocks away - one of the most spectacular fall displays of any tree.

idTips.label: Apricot-like seeds
idTips.description: Female trees produce orange, plum-sized seeds that smell absolutely terrible when they fall and start to rot - like rancid butter mixed with vomit. The inner nut is edible when cooked, though.

idTips.label: Distinctive bark
idTips.description: Mature trees develop deeply furrowed, grayish bark with a corky texture that feels rough and deeply ridged under your fingers.

habitat: In New England, you'll find ginkgos almost exclusively as planted ornamental trees in urban and suburban settings. They're popular street trees, park specimens, and landscape plants because they tolerate city pollution, compacted soil, and harsh growing conditions. With only 2 recorded observations in New England, they're quite rare as planted specimens here compared to other regions.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge bright green in late spring, unfurling from buds in their characteristic clustered arrangement on short spurs.
seasonality.summer: The distinctive fan-shaped leaves are fully developed and bright green, making identification straightforward during the growing season.
seasonality.fall: This is peak ginkgo season - the entire tree turns brilliant golden-yellow virtually overnight, then drops all its leaves within a few days. Female trees produce smelly orange seeds.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches show the characteristic spur-like short shoots where leaves were clustered, and mature trees display their distinctive deeply furrowed bark.

funFact: Some ginkgo trees in Japan are over 3,500 years old, making them among the oldest living things on Earth - they were already ancient when the pyramids were built, and several ginkgo trees actually survived the atomic bomb blast in Hiroshima and are still growing today!
confusionNotes: The fan-shaped leaves make ginkgo nearly impossible to confuse with any other tree, but beginners sometimes mistake the leaves for those of maidenhair ferns when they first fall. Remember: if it's on a tree, it's definitely ginkgo - maidenhair ferns are small ground plants.
contextualKnowledge: Ginkgo is often misspelled as "gingko," but the correct spelling has no 'g' in the middle. Be aware that female trees produce seeds with an incredibly offensive smell, so many cities only plant male trees. This is one of the few trees where you definitely want to know the sex before planting!
compareHints: Ginkgo is the sole survivor of its entire order - it literally has no close relatives left alive on Earth. The closest living relatives are actually cycads, those palm-like plants that look nothing like ginkgo. Among familiar trees, ginkgo's parallel-veined, fan-shaped leaves are completely unique - no other tree has anything remotely similar.
